cues.text: Hey, welcome back.
A balloon feels smooth from outside, but inside, molecules are constantly
moving and striking its walls.
Kinetic theory connects that microscopic motion to the pressure and temperature
we measure.
Begin with the ideal gas equation: pressure times volume equals the number of
moles times R times absolute temperature.
We can also write it as the number of molecules times Boltzmann's constant
times temperature.
These are the same equation expressed with different ways of counting
particles.
Avogadro's constant is about six point zero two two times ten to the power
twenty three particles per mole.
Multiply the number of moles by it to get the number of molecules.
R equals Avogadro's constant times Boltzmann's constant.
Let's take one mole at three hundred kelvin in zero point zero two five cubic
metres.
With R eight point three one four, pressure is one times eight point three one
four times three hundred, divided by zero point zero two five.
That is about ninety nine thousand seven hundred and sixty eight pascals.
Don't mix molecule count with the molar gas constant.
And never put Celsius directly into the gas equation.
The ideal gas model treats particles as very small compared with their
separation and neglects intermolecular forces except during collisions.
It is an approximation, especially useful for dilute gases.
Why do moving molecules produce pressure?
A molecule that strikes a wall changes its momentum.
The wall exerts an impulse on the molecule, and the molecule exerts the
opposite impulse on the wall.
Count many collisions per second and you obtain a steady average force.
Divide by wall area to get pressure.
For random isotropic motion, the average squared speed is shared equally among
three perpendicular directions.
This gives pressure equal to one third of gas density times mean square speed.
The square root of mean square speed is called RMS speed.
Combining the pressure relation with the gas equation gives average
translational kinetic energy per molecule equal to three halves times
Boltzmann's constant times temperature.
So temperature measures the energy scale of random translational motion, not
the speed of every molecule.
At the same temperature, a nitrogen molecule and a helium atom have the same
average translational kinetic energy in the ideal model.
Since their masses differ, their typical speeds differ.
Pause on that distinction.
Equal average kinetic energy does not mean equal RMS speed.
Also, translational energy is not always all the internal energy.
Molecules may rotate or vibrate, which adds other contributions.
Our derivation assumes elastic collisions, negligible particle volume and
random equilibrium motion.
A gas flowing rapidly as a whole needs its bulk motion distinguished from its
random thermal motion.
Now let's calculate a speed.
RMS speed is the square root of three R T divided by molar mass.
For nitrogen at three hundred kelvin, use molar mass zero point zero two eight
kilograms per mole, not twenty eight.
With R eight point three one four, the result is about five hundred and
seventeen metres per second.
That is surprisingly fast, but remember the directions keep changing through
collisions.
The gas does not cross the room as one organized team.
In many JEE questions, ratios are faster than full substitution.
For the same gas, speed scales with the square root of absolute temperature.
Warming it from three hundred to twelve hundred kelvin makes RMS speed twice as
large, not four times.
At the same temperature, speed scales inversely with the square root of
particle mass.
Helium has molar mass four grams per mole, while nitrogen has twenty eight.
Their RMS speed ratio is the square root of twenty eight divided by four, which
is the square root of seven.
Helium is faster.
RMS speed, average speed and most probable speed are different statistical
quantities; a question naming one of them requires its matching formula.
Individual particles have a range of speeds.
And the average velocity of an equilibrium gas at rest is zero even though its
average speed and RMS speed are not.
Why do different gases need different amounts of energy for the same
temperature rise?
They can store energy in different kinds of motion.
Classical equipartition assigns half k B T per molecule to each active
quadratic energy term.
Count these terms as f, the degrees of freedom.
A monatomic ideal gas has three translational terms, giving internal energy
three halves n R T.
A diatomic molecule can also rotate.
In the familiar rigid diatomic approximation with vibration inactive, we use
five active degrees of freedom.
The constant volume molar heat capacity is f R divided by two.
For an ideal gas, the constant pressure molar heat capacity is larger by R,
because heating at constant pressure also allows expansion work.
That gives gamma, the ratio of the two capacities, as f plus two divided by f.
Monatomic gamma is five thirds.
Rigid diatomic gamma is seven fifths.
Let's warm two moles of a monatomic ideal gas by ten kelvin at fixed volume.
Multiply two by three halves R by ten: thirty R, about two hundred and forty
nine point four two joules.
These are molar heat capacities in joules per mole per kelvin, not specific
heat per kilogram.
Real molecular modes can freeze out or become active with temperature, so f and
heat capacities are not universal constants across every temperature range.
Let's connect molecular theory back to work.
Compress a gas from three litres to one litre against a constant external
pressure of one hundred thousand pascals.
Work by the gas is external pressure times the final minus initial volume.
The change is minus zero point zero zero two cubic metres, so work by the gas
is minus two hundred joules.
The surroundings do positive two hundred joules of work on it.
The first law still tells us how this work and any heat exchange change
internal energy.
Another microscopic quantity is mean free path: the average distance a molecule
travels between successive collisions.
In a dilute hard sphere model, it equals one divided by the square root of two,
times pi, times molecular diameter squared, times number density.
Number density means molecules per volume, not moles per volume.
Doubling number density while holding diameter fixed halves the mean free path.
Doubling the molecular diameter quarters it.
If an ideal gas is held at fixed temperature and its pressure doubles, its
number density doubles, so this model predicts half the mean free path.
This is an average, not an identical straight path assigned to every molecule.
Use consistent SI units and distinguish mass density from number density.
Those distinctions connect the microscopic picture to reliable calculations.
